analysis.one_liner: Gives a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for donations to private-school scholarship funds.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2025 with two cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without any action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a federal tax credit for people and corporations who give money to nonprofit scholarship organizations that pay for private school tuition, tutoring, homeschooling costs, and related expenses. Donors get back every dollar they give (up to $5,000 per year for individuals, or more for high earners), effectively redirecting their federal taxes into a $10 billion-a-year national pool for private and religious education. The scholarships themselves are tax-free to the families receiving them.
analysis.who_benefits: Donors with federal income tax bills: the credit is dollar-for-dollar but cannot exceed taxes owed, so those who can use it fully are households owing at least $5,000 in tax and corporations. Families already in or seeking private school, homeschooling, or tutoring get a new funding stream. Private and religious schools and the scholarship organizations that administer the money gain a large, permanent federal funding channel.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals get a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for contributions to scholarship granting organizations, up to the greater of 10% of adjusted gross income or $5,000 per year [S2].
Corporations get a credit for such contributions, capped at 5% of taxable income [S2].
Scholarship amounts paid to students are excluded from taxable income [S2].

Scholarships cover tuition, fees, curricula, tutoring, standardized and admissions test fees, dual college enrollment, therapies for students with disabilities, transportation, and homeschooling expenses [S2].

A national volume cap starts at $10 billion per year, allocated to states partly by school-age population and partly by child poverty, and grows 5% after any year in which 90% of the cap is used [S2].
Scholarship organizations must prioritize students who received scholarships the prior year, then their siblings, then students from households below 500% of the poverty line [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a group, since up to $10 billion a year in credits (growing over time) is revenue the Treasury never collects. Public schools face enrollment losses and a politically financed competitor for students, since federal tax dollars now flow to private and religious schools with no requirement that those schools meet public accountability rules.

drawbacks.text: The credit is nonrefundable, so only taxpayers with at least $5,000 in federal tax liability can use the full amount; households with little or no tax bill cannot donate at their own expense at all, meaning the largest subsidies go to the highest earners [S2].

The priority rules put returning scholarship students and their siblings ahead of lower-income applicants, and the income priority extends to families earning up to 500% of the poverty line, so the money is not targeted mainly at poor children [S2].

The bill bars any federal, state, or local government from controlling any aspect of scholarship organizations or private and religious schools, and forbids excluding schools based on religious policies, leaving no accountability conditions on where the subsidized money goes [S2].

Scholarship organizations may keep up to 10% of receipts for administrative expenses, and must distribute the rest within three years, so up to $1 billion a year of the initial cap can go to overhead [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some families genuinely get help paying for private school, tutoring, or disability therapies, and parents who want those options gain real purchasing power. But the design channels the biggest benefit to donors with large tax bills, sends federal revenue to private and religious schools with no accountability requirements, and leaves the volume cap growing automatically. Public schools lose students and political ground without receiving anything in return.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two committees, and neither has taken it up, so it is sitting without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Burgess Owens introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee [S4].
The bill's only cosponsors are two House Republicans [S3].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor action has occurred since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet because the bill has not moved; so far federal revenue and public schools are unaffected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill comes from a Republican with two Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors, but no votes have occurred, so the party split has not been tested.

industries.note: The bill routes up to $10 billion a year in federal tax credits through scholarship organizations to pay private and religious school tuition, and bars governments from imposing any conditions on those schools, making them permanent recipients of federal education dollars.

These nonprofits become the mandatory middleman for the entire program and can retain up to 10% of contributions for administration, giving them a large revenue stream tied to the program's continuation.

Donors with sufficient tax liability convert owed federal taxes into directed donations, a dollar-for-dollar reduction in their tax bill; families with little tax liability cannot use the credit at all.
Public schools gain nothing from the bill but face enrollment competition from federally subsidized private options and the political erosion that follows.

analysis.trajectory: With two cosponsors, no committee action in months, and a tax provision requiring action by the Ways and Means Committee, the bill is likely to die quietly. An identical or similar scholarship tax credit could still advance only as part of a much larger tax package, not on its own.
